blocks.h: Hot, ambient, ozonated or cold: choosing microbial control
rows: Continuous temperature; the FDA inspection guide calls hot 65–80 °C systems self-sanitizing
Hot WFI from a still, the example Annex 1, 6.10 gives
Simplest to defend. Costs insulation, holding energy, point-of-use coolers and the highest rouge risk.
Hot water sanitization on a predetermined schedule, proven at the coldest probe
PW; membrane WFI where your contamination control strategy (CCS) justifies ambient storage
Lower energy. The loop is out of use for each cycle, and heat still drives rouge.
Ozone held in the tank and destroyed by UV; UV off on a schedule to sanitize the loop
PW and membrane WFI where heat cycles are unwanted
No heat cycles or heat-rated piping. Needs ozone measured at three points, absent at use, safe venting and compatible seals.
Slows growth but does not kill; periodic heat or ozone sanitizes
Processes that need chilled water at the point of use
Chiller load, condensation and longer cycles. Choose it for the process, not microbial control.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Does a WFI loop have to be hot?
items.a: Not by rule: Annex 1, 6.10 gives circulation above 70 °C only as an example. Ambient WFI loops with ozone or periodic heat are in use, if your CCS justifies the choice and monitoring supports it. With a still, a hot loop is usually simplest to defend; with membrane WFI, energy often favours ambient. We set out both.

items.q: Which L/D do you design to, and how do you measure it?
items.a: L/D ≤ 2, the ASME BPE target: L from the inside wall of the main pipe to the valve seal point, D the branch inside diameter, at every tee and sample valve too. We do not design to the six-diameter rule of the FDA's 1993 guide, written for hot 75–80 °C systems. Every branch is in the dead leg register.

items.q: How do you keep flow turbulent when several points of use open at once?
items.a: We size pipe and pump for the worst-case combination of outlets from your survey, not the average. A variable speed pump holds return flow or pressure, and a low-return-flow alarm tells you when it cannot. At SAT we open those outlets together and record return flow: the qualified rate Annex 1, 6.9 asks you to monitor.

items.q: How do you prove there is no ozone at the point of use?
items.a: An ozone sensor after the UV destruct unit is interlocked to stop supply on breakthrough, and UV intensity is monitored. After each loop sanitization the water is tested for residual ozone before use, as Annex 1, 6.12 asks for testing after disinfection. The interlock is tested at FAT and OQ.

items.q: How should points of use be sampled?
items.a: The way the water is used: if a hose is usually attached, the FDA guide says sample at its end. Annex 1, 6.13 asks for all outlets at a set interval and a representative sample daily. We write this into the performance qualification (PQ) protocol; Annex 1, 6.8 expects seasonal variation, so plan PQ data over a year.

Rouge, the iron oxide film on stainless steel, forms mainly in hot WFI, pure steam and heat-cycled systems. Loose rouge is a particle risk your quality unit will expect inspected and trended. We limit the causes at design (finish, passivation, chloride control, pump selection), add inspection points at the tank and pump, and plan derouging as maintenance.

items.q: Can you add points of use to an existing loop?
items.a: Yes, after a hydraulic check of the whole loop at the new peak draw. Each branch is cut in with a zero-static valve, orbitally welded, passivated and added to the isometrics and dead leg register under your change control. Shutdown depends on the tie-ins: [typical shutdown for a point-of-use addition, days]. See upgrades and requalification.

items.q: Can the loop connect to a generator from another supplier?
items.a: Yes. The functional specification defines the interface: water quality and flow at the tank inlet, the signals exchanged, and how a generator divert or low tank level is handled, so loop and generator are qualified as one system.
